lessons.culture: In Hejazi families, asking about relatives is a warm and immediate greeting, and people share family news openly. The greeting "السّلام عليكم" is used regularly among locals and visitors alike. Being married or single is discussed openly, and single status followed by "إن شاء الله" (God willing) is the respectful way to discuss future marriage prospects, reflecting religious and traditional values.

lessons.culture: Hejazi hospitality is generous, and hosts take pride in serving coffee and food to guests. The phrases "صحة وعافية" after someone finishes eating, and "بالعافية" while they are still eating, are always used and answered with "الله يعافيك". In the holy cities, religious phrases like "الحمد لله" (thank God) after eating are part of everyday courtesy, and people say "فوري" (right away) when serving or responding to requests.

lessons.culture: Guests in a Hejazi home are received in the "مجلس" near the entrance, and the guest room is kept ready and separate from the family rooms. "الحمام" is the bathroom or toilet, and in old houses a flat roof "سطح" and a balcony with wooden lattice "روشان" are common.

exercises.prompt: Someone asks you: "فين المطبخ؟" Say it is next to the majlis.

too_formal.feedback: This is correct formal Arabic, but everyday Hejazi speech says "جنب المجلس".

exercises.tip: "جنب" means next to.

exercises.prompt: Someone asks you: "فين الحمام؟" Say in the corridor, on the right.

too_formal.feedback: This is correct formal Arabic, but everyday Hejazi speech says "في الممر، على اليمين".

exercises.tip: "اليمين" is the right and "الشمال" is the left.

exercises.prompt: Someone asks you: "أوضة الضيوف جاهزة؟" Say yes, it is ready.

too_formal.feedback: This is correct formal Arabic, but everyday Hejazi speech says "إيوه، جاهزة".

exercises.tip: "أوضة" is feminine, so "جاهزة".

exercises.prompt: Complete: "أوض النوم _____." Meaning: The bedrooms are upstairs.

too_formal.feedback: This is correct formal Arabic, but everyday Hejazi speech says "فوق".

exercises.tip: "فوق" is up or above; "تحت" is down.

exercises.prompt: Complete: "المجلس _____." Meaning: The majlis is downstairs.

too_formal.feedback: This is correct formal Arabic, but everyday Hejazi speech says "تحت".

exercises.tip: "تحت" is down or below.

exercises.prompt: Translate: "Go to the garden." (to a man)

too_formal.feedback: This is correct formal Arabic, but everyday Hejazi speech says "روح الجنينة".

exercises.tip: "روح" is "go" in Hejazi speech.

exercises.prompt: Translate: "Let us go up to the roof."

too_formal.feedback: This is correct formal Arabic, but everyday Hejazi speech says "يلا نطلع السطح".

exercises.tip: "طلع" means go up.

exercises.prompt: Translate: "Where are the stairs?"

too_formal.feedback: This is correct formal Arabic, but everyday Hejazi speech says "فين الدرج؟".

exercises.tip: "درج" is the stairs.

exercises.prompt: Which word means "behind"?

too_formal.feedback: This is correct formal Arabic, but everyday Hejazi speech says "ورا".

exercises.tip: "ورا" is behind and "قدام" is in front.

exercises.prompt: Which word means "corridor"?

too_formal.feedback: This is correct formal Arabic, but everyday Hejazi speech says "ممر".

exercises.tip: "ممر" is the corridor; "سطح" is the roof.

exercises.prompt: Which phrase means "ground floor"?

too_formal.feedback: This is correct formal Arabic, but everyday Hejazi speech says "دور تحت".

exercises.tip: "تحت" is lower and "فوق" is upper.

exercises.prompt: Put these words in a natural order: "مسكّر / الباب"

too_formal.feedback: This is correct formal Arabic, but everyday Hejazi speech says "الباب مسكّر".

exercises.tip: "مسكّر" means shut.

exercises.prompt: Put these words in a natural order: "النوم / جنب / أوضة / البلكونة"

too_formal.feedback: This is correct formal Arabic, but everyday Hejazi speech says "البلكونة جنب أوضة النوم".

exercises.tip: "أوضة النوم" is the bedroom.

dialogue.speaker: Yasser
dialogue.english: Okay. But it is very hot.

dialogue.speaker: Amina
dialogue.english: The blanket is in the wardrobe.

lessons.culture: Hejazi homes are often cooled by air-conditioning, and a "مروحة" (fan) is used in older houses and on the roof in the evening. Everyday objects keep borrowed names in speech, such as "ريموت" (remote control) and "لمبة" (lamp), and the sofa is "كنبة".

exercises.prompt: Someone asks you: "فين الريموت؟" Say it is on the table.

too_formal.feedback: This is correct formal Arabic, but everyday Hejazi speech says "على الطاولة".

exercises.tip: "على" means on.

exercises.prompt: Someone asks you: "إيش تحتاج؟" Say you need a blanket.

too_formal.feedback: This is correct formal Arabic, but everyday Hejazi speech says "أنا محتاج بطانية".

exercises.tip: A woman says "محتاجة".

exercises.prompt: Someone asks you: "الغسالة تشتغل؟" Say no, it does not work.

too_formal.feedback: This is correct formal Arabic, but everyday Hejazi speech says "لا، ما تشتغل".

exercises.tip: "ما" before the verb makes it negative.

exercises.prompt: Complete: "_____ الضو." Meaning: Switch on the light.

too_formal.feedback: This is correct formal Arabic, but everyday Hejazi speech says "شغّل".

exercises.tip: "شغّل" means switch on or start.

exercises.prompt: Complete: "_____ الشباك." Meaning: Close the window.

too_formal.feedback: This is correct formal Arabic, but everyday Hejazi speech says "سكّر".

exercises.tip: "سكّر" is to close.

exercises.prompt: Translate: "Switch off the light." (to a man)

too_formal.feedback: This is correct formal Arabic, but everyday Hejazi speech says "طفّي الضو".

exercises.tip: "طفّي" is switch off or put out.

exercises.prompt: Translate: "Open the window." (to a man)

too_formal.feedback: This is correct formal Arabic, but everyday Hejazi speech says "افتح الشباك".

exercises.tip: "شباك" is the everyday word for window.

exercises.prompt: Translate: "The mirror is next to the door."

too_formal.feedback: This is correct formal Arabic, but everyday Hejazi speech says "المراية جنب الباب".

exercises.tip: "مراية" is a mirror.

exercises.prompt: Which word means "fan"?

too_formal.feedback: This is correct formal Arabic, but everyday Hejazi speech says "مروحة".

exercises.tip: "مروحة" is a fan; "لمبة" is a lamp.

exercises.prompt: Which word means "remote control"?

too_formal.feedback: This is correct formal Arabic, but everyday Hejazi speech says "ريموت".

exercises.tip: "ريموت" is borrowed from English.

exercises.prompt: Put these words in a natural order: "تشتغل / ما / الغسالة"

too_formal.feedback: This is correct formal Arabic, but everyday Hejazi speech says "الغسالة ما تشتغل".

exercises.tip: "ما" comes before the verb.

exercises.prompt: Put these words in a natural order: "المفتاح / فين"

too_formal.feedback: This is correct formal Arabic, but everyday Hejazi speech says "فين المفتاح".

exercises.tip: "فين" comes first.

challenge.title: Meeting Family Over a Meal
challenge.instructions: Write and say a short Hejazi conversation that lasts at least 10 lines. It must include a question about someone's family, a description of at least one relative, a statement of hunger or thirst, ordering or offering food and drink, one of the fixed exchanges (بِالْعَافِيَة / اللَّهُ يُعَافِيك or صِحَّة وَعَافِيَة / اللَّهُ يُعَافِيك), and asking for the bill. Use at least 8 target phrases from Unit 2 and include both a masculine-address form and a feminine-address form.
required_elements: A question about family using كَمْ نَاسِ فِي أَهْلِك؟ or similar.
A description of at least one family member using أمي, أبوي, أخوي, أختي, زوجي, مرتي, ولدي, or بنتي.
A statement of hunger or thirst using جوعان, جوعانة, or عطشان.
An order or offer of food or drink using أبي آكل or أبي اشرب.
One of the fixed exchanges: بِالْعَافِيَة / اللَّهُ يُعَافِيك, or صِحَّة وَعَافِيَة / اللَّهُ يُعَافِيك.
A request for the bill using الْحِسَاب لَوْ سَمَحْت or كَمْ الْحِسَاب؟
Both a masculine-address form (such as كَمْ نَاسِ فِي أَهْلِك؟) and a feminine-address form (such as كَمْ نَاسِ فِي أَهْلِك؟).

dialogue.speaker: مُحَمَّد
dialogue.english: Peace be upon you, how are you, Fatima?

dialogue.speaker: فَاطِمَة
dialogue.arabic: وَعَلَيْكُمُ السَّلَامُ وَرَحْمَةُ اللَّهِ، بِخَيْر الْحَمْدُ لِلَّهِ.
dialogue.transliteration: w 3alaykum assalaam w ra7ma allah, bikhayr il7amdulillah.
dialogue.english: And upon you be peace and God's mercy, well, praise be to God.

dialogue.speaker: مُحَمَّد
dialogue.english: How many people in your family?

dialogue.speaker: فَاطِمَة
dialogue.english: I have my brother and two sisters. And you?

dialogue.speaker: مُحَمَّد
dialogue.english: I have my wife and three children.

dialogue.speaker: فَاطِمَة
dialogue.english: I'm very hungry, do you want to eat something?

dialogue.speaker: فَاطِمَة
dialogue.english: And what do you want to drink?
